questions.stem: A colourless gas relights a glowing splint. The gas is
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so a splint that is merely glowing bursts back into flame in a jar of it. This is the standard confirmatory test for oxygen.

distractorRationale.a: Hydrogen burns itself with a pop when a lighted splint is applied, but it does not support the combustion of the splint
distractorRationale.c: Carbon dioxide puts out a burning splint rather than relighting it
distractorRationale.d: Nitrogen is unreactive and also extinguishes a burning splint

questions.stem: Why is ammonia dried with quicklime rather than with concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid?

options.text: Concentrated H2SO4 is a liquid and cannot dry any gas
Ammonia is basic and would react with the acid to form ammonium sulphate
Quicklime dries gases faster than any other drying agent
Ammonia is denser than air, so an acid drier would not work

questions.explanation: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas. Passing it through concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid would neutralise it: 2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4, so the gas would be absorbed instead of dried. Quicklime, calcium oxide, removes water without reacting with a base.

distractorRationale.a: Concentrated H2SO4 is in fact the standard drying agent for most gases, used in a wash bottle
distractorRationale.c: Speed is not the issue; the choice is driven entirely by chemical compatibility
distractorRationale.d: Ammonia is less dense than air, and density affects collection, not drying

questions.stem: Which pair of reagents is used for the laboratory preparation of carbon dioxide?

options.text: Marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid
Marble chips and dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid
Zinc granules and dilute hydrochloric acid
Iron(II) sulphide and dilute hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: Marble is calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) and reacts steadily with dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The calcium chloride formed is soluble, so fresh acid keeps reaching the marble and the reaction continues.

distractorRationale.b: This starts well but stops quickly, because insoluble calcium sulphate coats the marble and blocks further reaction
distractorRationale.c: This is the standard preparation of hydrogen, not carbon dioxide
distractorRationale.d: Iron(II) sulphide with acid gives hydrogen sulphide

questions.stem: Two colourless gases each turn limewater milky. Which further test distinguishes sulphur(IV) oxide from carbon dioxide?

options.text: Only sulphur(IV) oxide turns acidified dichromate solution from orange to green
Only carbon dioxide turns damp blue litmus paper red
Only sulphur(IV) oxide extinguishes a burning splint
Only carbon dioxide is denser than air

questions.explanation: Sulphur(IV) oxide is a reducing agent. It reduces orange dichromate to green chromium(III) ions while itself being oxidised to sulphate. Carbon dioxide has no reducing power because carbon is already at its maximum oxidation number of +4, so the dichromate stays orange.

distractorRationale.b: Both gases are acidic oxides and both turn damp blue litmus red, so this cannot separate them
distractorRationale.c: Neither gas supports combustion, so both put out a burning splint
distractorRationale.d: Both gases are denser than air, so density is no help here

questions.stem: In the Contact process, sulphur(VI) oxide is absorbed in concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid rather than in water because

options.text: sulphur(VI) oxide does not react with water at all
direct absorption in water forms a dense acid mist that is difficult to condense
water would reduce the sulphur(VI) oxide back to sulphur(IV) oxide
the acid produced would be too dilute to be of any use

questions.explanation: SO3 reacts with water so vigorously and exothermically that it produces a fine acid mist that will not condense and escapes from the plant. Absorbing it in concentrated acid to form oleum, H2S2O7, and then diluting that oleum with water gives controlled, safe production.

distractorRationale.a: It reacts with water very readily indeed; that is precisely the problem
distractorRationale.c: Water is not a reducing agent and cannot reverse the oxidation
distractorRationale.d: The concentration could easily be adjusted; the real obstacle is the uncontrollable mist

questions.stem: Dense white fumes are seen when a gas is brought near the mouth of a bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid. The gas is
questions.explanation: Ammonia reacts with hydrogen chloride vapour to form solid ammonium chloride, whose tiny suspended particles appear as dense white fumes: NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl. It is the classic test for ammonia and works because both substances are volatile.

distractorRationale.a: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow acidic gas and gives no white fumes with hydrochloric acid
distractorRationale.c: Sulphur(IV) oxide is acidic, so it does not react with an acid to form a salt
distractorRationale.d: Hydrogen sulphide is also acidic and gives no reaction with hydrochloric acid

questions.stem: Ammonia is collected over water because it is only slightly soluble.
questions.explanation: False. Ammonia is extremely soluble in water, which is why the fountain experiment works, so collecting it over water would simply dissolve it. Because it is also less dense than air it is collected by downward delivery into an inverted gas jar.

questions.stem: Which of the following gases contribute directly to acid rain? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Acid rain is caused by acidic oxides dissolving in rainwater. Sulphur(IV) oxide from burning sulphur-containing fuels gives trioxosulphate(IV) and eventually tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, and nitrogen(IV) oxide formed in hot engines gives trioxonitrate(V) acid.

distractorRationale.c: Carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide and forms no acid with water; it is dangerous as a poison, not as an acidifier
distractorRationale.d: Ammonia is alkaline, so it neutralises acidity rather than causing it

questions.stem: Which of the following is the laboratory preparation method for hydrogen chloride gas?

options.text: Reacting concentrated hydrochloric acid with sodium bicarbonate
Reacting concentrated hydrochloric acid with zinc

Reacting sodium chloride with sulfuric acid

distractorRationale.b: This reaction produces hydrogen gas, not hydrogen chloride.
